Living in the Spotlight 

 The Journey of Avraham & Yitzchak 

 VS. Hagar and Ishmael
sheets.summary: This shiur is based on a talk by Rabbi Menachem Penner comparing the Torah readings of Rosh Hashana- the story of Hagar and Yishmael vs. that of Abraham and Yitzchak. The main difference he says is in their mindset: Hagar did not see her journey as purposeful. The spotlight was on Avraham's home but she just a cast away. Little did she know the story and blessing that she and her family will receive. God had a Divine plan specifically for her... and so too, it is with all of us.

With the Waxing Moon... 	we will connect to personal and collective legacies of resilience

With the Full Moon… 	we will immerse in alternative Jewish histories of gender

description.en: The Hebrew word for ritual sacrifice is “korban,” or that which is brought near — to be offered to God. The Torah, mainly in the [book of Leviticus](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus?tab=contents), describes different kinds of offerings for different occasions and circumstances, and the ancient rabbis discuss sacrifices in detail in the fifth order of the Mishnah, [Kodashim](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Mishnah/Seder%20Kodashim), and later in the Talmud. Among the many kinds of sacrifices are those given in regular service to God, for giving thanks, to atone for sin, on the occasion of presenting oneself at the Temple in Jerusalem, for holidays, and more.

The "Ten Commandments" or "Ten Utterances" are the group of the commandments given to the Israelites at Mount Sinai in a constitutive moment of divine revelation to all of the children of Israel. The first set of five commandments establish the rules of God's relationship with humanity, and the second set of five are between people and other people. The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah: first, when they are given at Sinai, in [Exodus 20](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.20?lang=bi&aliyot=0) and again in [Deuteronomy 5](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.5.7?lang=bi&aliyot=0), in Moses' retelling of the earlier narrative.

description.en: The Torah is Judaism's foundational text, described as given by God to the people of Israel at Mount Sinai. The five books that make up the Torah are [Genesis](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis?tab=contents), [Exodus](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus?tab=contents), [Leviticus](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus?tab=contents), [Numbers](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers?tab=contents), and [Deuteronomy](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy?tab=contents). They tell of the origins and development of the Israelite nation and present the foundational laws of Judaism. In some contexts, “Torah” refers broadly to both the Written and Oral Torah, which includes not only the five books of the Torah but the entire Tanakh (Hebrew Bible), rabbinic literature, and any interpretations relating to those texts.

description.en: *Avodat Hashem* — ”service of God” in English — is a primary religious objective in many Jewish texts. The first use of the term “service” in relationship to people serving God is in the book of Exodus, describing the expected [worship](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.7.16?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) of the Israelites upon leaving Egypt. In later Jewish sources, *avodat Hashem* takes the form of ritual sacrifices, prayer, general fulfillment of the Torah’s commandments, or ethical character development.

description.en: Joseph Karo, expelled from Spain as a child, was a rabbi, talmudist, mystic, and preemiment halakhic codifier. His best-known work, the Shulchan Arukh, was accepted in his lifetime and formally recognized thereafter as the definitive statement of Jewish legal and religious practice. He also wrote basic commentaries on Rambam's Mishneh Torah and Jacob ben Ashe's Arba'ah Turim, both of which were major sources for his own Shulchan Arukh. As a mystic, he also received heavenly revelations. Some of these were set down in writing and contributed to his decision to migrate to the land of Israel. There, he lived in Safed, where he supported the effort of his teacher, Rabbi Yaakov Berav, to revive traditional rabbinic ordination (Hebrew: semikhah).

description.en: The morning prayer service in Judaism—*Shacharit* in Hebrew—consists of four main sections: preparatory prayers and readings; the [Shema](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shema?tab=admin) and its blessings; the [Amidah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemoneh-esrei?sort=Relevance&tab=admin); and the concluding sections. The Torah is read on Mondays, Thursdays, and Shabbat, as well as on most other special days. Rabbinic sources delve into the origins and significance of daily morning prayers.
description.he: שחרית היא תפילת הבוקר. בתפילה זו כלולים ארבעה חלקים עיקריים: קטעי הכנה וקריאה מקדימים, קריאת שמע וברכותיה, תפילת עמידה (שמונה־עשרה) וקטעי סיום. התורה נקראת בימים שני וחמישי, בשבת ובמועדים.
